questions.q: How are elements of a standard array arranged in computer memory?
options: In contiguous memory cells placed one after another.
In scattered heap blocks connected by pointer links.
In alternating cache rows indexed through hashing functions.
questions.fact: An array stores elements in contiguous memory.
why: Arrays reserve adjacent memory cells so any index is directly reachable.
Scattered blocks linked by pointers describe linked lists, not arrays.
Arrays use sequential memory addresses rather than hashed cache blocks.

questions.q: In an array of length n, what is the index of the final element?
options: The final index is always n.
The final index is length − 1.
The final index is length + 1.
questions.fact: Indexing starts at 0; the last valid index is length − 1.
why: Index n is out of bounds because indexing begins at zero.
Because indices count from 0, the n-th element sits at length − 1.
Length + 1 exceeds the allocated range of the array.

questions.q: Which formula calculates the memory address of the element at index i in an array?
options: address(i) = base_address + i
address(i) = base_address × i + element_size
address(i) = base_address + i × element_size
why: Adding i directly ignores the byte width of each element.
Multiplying the base address corrupts the memory location.
The offset is index times element size added to base address.

questions.q: What is the time complexity to update a value at a known index in an array?
options: O(1) constant time.
O(log n) logarithmic time.
O(n) linear time.
questions.fact: Updating an element at a known index is O(1).
why: The exact address is computed immediately without shifting any other items.
No binary search is involved because the index is already known.
No elements shift when overwriting an existing slot at a known index.

questions.q: When inserting an element into an array, in which order must existing items shift right?
options: From the insertion point forward toward the end.
Starting from the end backwards to avoid overwriting values.
Simultaneously using temporary memory buffers for all values.
questions.fact: When inserting, elements are shifted starting from the end so that no value is overwritten.
why: Shifting forward would overwrite adjacent elements before they can be copied.
Starting from the end frees the next slot before moving into it.
In-place shifts do not require allocating duplicate memory buffers.

questions.q: Why does deleting an element from the middle of an array take O(n) time?
options: Memory deallocation must search each preceding element pointer.
The entire array must be reallocated into new heap space.
Later elements must shift left to close the vacated gap.
questions.fact: Deletion in the middle is O(n) because later elements must shift left.
why: Arrays store contiguous values without individual node pointers.
Deletion happens within the existing allocation without creating a new array.
To maintain contiguous order, every subsequent element shifts left one position.

questions.q: What is the worst-case time complexity of linear search on an array?
options: O(n) because every element may need to be inspected.
O(log n) because the search range is repeatedly halved.
O(1) because direct index calculation locates the target instantly.
questions.fact: Linear search checks elements one by one and is O(n).
why: In the worst case, the target is at the end or missing.
Halving the range requires sorted order and binary search, not linear.
Direct index lookup requires knowing the index beforehand, not searching.
